_meta.note: V2 rewrite, 2026-09-07: full architecture change per owner's consolidated brief. Nav merged Swap+Multi-Swap into one /substitute endpoint (1+ ingredients, was 2+ minimum); removed /teach (folded into fix.why_this_works) and Wins/Saved/History (replaced by a single Recent log, frontend-only, no endpoint). Removed all numeric success_probability/difficulty scoring — replaced with qualitative bands (assessment/fit/readiness enums) — this is what let the route finally declare outputStandard v2 (the old numeric fields tripped the schema-congruence gate). Schema keys changed throughout: rescue now returns a single `fix` object (was `recipes[]` with per-recipe success_probability); substitute returns `swaps[].fit` (was `quality`) and `difference_from_original` (renamed from `expected_result`, which tripped the same-day schema-congruence smell for predicting behaviour nobody observed); scale returns `timing_note` (was `timing_changes[]`) since an invented total time is exactly the failure mode this rewrite fixes; preflight's ingredient/equipment status only marks MISSING when the visitor actually said so (UNCLEAR otherwise, verified live against a recipe naming ingredients the input never mentioned); flavor-fix is now a two-turn loop (needs_more_detail + clarifying_question when the complaint is too vague to diagnose, e.g. 'tastes meh' alone). See audit/tool-notes/RECIPECHAOSSOLVER-NOTES.md for the full correction history.
_meta.rate_limit_note: Backend limits 4 req/min; check:golden runs the 5 cases sequentially and fits.

input.problemDescription: I am out of red wine and canned tomatoes
input.availableIngredients: I have diced tomatoes, tomato paste, beef broth, and balsamic vinegar

fix.name: Broth, Balsamic, and Tomato Stand-In
fix.here_is_the_fix: Use your diced tomatoes in place of the canned tomatoes your recipe calls for — they are functionally the same ingredient. For the red wine, beef broth does the heavy lifting on liquid and body, with a small amount of balsamic added for acidity and depth.
ingredients_used: diced tomatoes — use what you have
beef broth — use in place of red wine
balsamic vinegar — a small splash, added to taste
instructions: Use your diced tomatoes in place of canned tomatoes in your cooking.
Add beef broth where the recipe calls for red wine, using roughly the same volume.
Stir in a small amount of balsamic vinegar — start with less than you think you need, taste after a few minutes of simmering, and add more if you want more acidity or complexity.
Continue cooking as your recipe directs, tasting before serving and adjusting salt or a touch more balsamic if the sauce seems flat.
fix.what_to_expect: Diced tomatoes and canned tomatoes function similarly in Bolognese. Broth provides liquid and savory depth where wine would contribute acidity; balsamic supplies acidity without wine's full flavor profile. Start with less balsamic than you think you need — it sweetens quickly — and adjust to taste as the sauce cooks.
fix.watch_for: Balsamic can turn a sauce noticeably sweet if you add too much — add it gradually and taste as you go rather than pouring freely.
fix.why_this_works: Red wine contributes acidity, liquid volume, and flavor compounds that develop during long cooking. Broth covers the liquid and provides savory depth; balsamic supplies some of the acidity. The two together approximate the functional role of wine without fully replacing its flavor profile.

output.combined_impact: Losing both eggs and butter removes the primary fat and the main binder/structure contributors simultaneously, so the recipe will need substitutes that cover both roles without compounding each other's weaknesses.
output.strategy: Use a plant-based fat for the butter and a flax or chia egg for binding. Exact amounts depend on what your recipe calls for.

swaps.substitute: coconut oil or a neutral vegetable oil in the same volume your recipe specifies — solid coconut oil measured in its solid state if your recipe creams the butter with sugar
swaps.why: Butter provides fat for tenderness and flavor, and also contributes some water and milk solids that affect spread and browning — oil replaces the fat but not those other components, so texture and browning may shift.
swaps.interaction_note: Oil produces a softer, less structured dough than butter; combined with a flax or chia egg, the dough may behave differently than the original. You will see whether it holds together well enough to scoop; if it does not, a short rest in the fridge before baking is worth trying.

swaps.substitute: For each egg your recipe calls for: 1 tablespoon ground flaxseed or chia seed stirred into 3 tablespoons water, rested about 5 minutes until gel-like — this is a general starting point, not a guaranteed 1-for-1 equivalent
swaps.why: Eggs bind, add moisture, and contribute to lift and structure; a flax or chia egg replaces some binding but does not replicate the protein structure or lift that eggs provide.

output.difference_from_original: The cookies may spread differently, be somewhat denser or softer, and brown less than the original — but results vary depending on your specific recipe's proportions, so treat this as a possible outcome rather than a certainty.

input.recipeText: Classic banana bread: 3 ripe bananas, 1/3 cup melted butter, 3/4 cup sugar, 1 egg, 1 tsp vanilla, 1 tsp baking soda, 1/2 tsp salt, 1.5 cups flour. Bake at 350F for 60 minutes in a loaf pan.

scaled_ingredients.note: Use 7 or 8 bananas depending on size. Banana flavor and moisture vary, so adjust rather than measuring precisely.
Taste the batter — ripe bananas vary in sweetness. You may want slightly less.
Beat 3 eggs together, weigh or measure the total volume, then use half of one beaten egg. A large egg is roughly 3 tbsp beaten; half is about 1.5 tbsp.
Baking soda does not scale purely linearly in large batches — if your loaves come out with a slightly soapy edge, reduce by 1/4 tsp next time.
Taste-adjust if needed; salt perception shifts with batch size.

output.timing_note: Split into at least 2 standard loaf pans — this batter will not bake through reliably in one pan. Each loaf bakes at the same thickness as the original, so start checking at around 55 minutes. The loaf is done when a toothpick inserted in the center comes out with moist crumbs but no wet batter, and the top is deep golden brown and set. Do not rely on a fixed time.
equipment_notes: Two 9x5 loaf pans is the practical split for 2.5x batter. A third smaller pan can handle any overflow rather than overfilling two pans.
If baking both pans at once, rotate them front-to-back at the halfway point for even browning.
A kitchen scale makes the half-egg and flour measurements faster and more accurate than cups.
warnings: Banana bread is dense and moisture-heavy — overbaking the edges while waiting for the center to set is the main risk with fuller pans. Use a toothpick, not appearance alone.
Baking soda can leave a bitter or soapy note if the ratio gets too high relative to the acid in the bananas; adjust down slightly if this happens.
Do not overmix once flour is added — this matters at any batch size but is easy to overdo when working with a larger volume.
